# To the Kindhearted
# Reader.

It is a common custom to place a preface or dedication before all treatises and books that are published, partly to bring the work and the author into public renown, partly to obtain a patron, friend, protection, grace, and favor, and partly to give thanks for benefits either already shown or hoped for.

For these and similar conditions <note>original: "Conditionen"</note>, no preface <note>original: "Præfation"</note> is necessary in this case: for the subject matter itself—namely, the Secret Chancery and Council Chambers of Anhalt—in which the wretched Bohemian disaster <note>original: "Böhaimbische Vnfall." This refers to the 1620 Battle of White Mountain, a pivotal defeat for the Protestant cause that led to the exile of the "Winter King" Frederick V and the escalation of the Thirty Years' War.</note> and, because of it, the misery currently unfolding before our eyes in German and other lands, as well as a nearly universal movement <note>original: "ac motus quasi universalis"</note> were debated, consulted upon, decided, and truly put into action. Likewise, [no preface is needed because] such hidden, important secrets <note>original: "Secreta"</note>, which unexpectedly

# To the Kindhearted
[Reader,]

come to the light of day: has become so famous and resounded in such a way that almost everyone has conceived a special, eager longing to know of it.

The authors of such secret matters—namely Prince Christian of Anhalt <note>Christian I, Prince of Anhalt-Bernburg (1568–1630), was the chief advisor to the Elector Palatine and a lead diplomat for the Protestant Union.</note>, the Elector Palatine <note>original: "Churpfaltz"</note>, Margrave Joachim Ernst of Brandenburg, Albrecht Count of Solms, Volrath von Plessen, Dr. Ludwig Camerarius, etc., Achatz and Christoph von Dohna, etc.—are already well known in their own right. Some, despite their lower social status, have become famous because of these Bohemian and related functions <term>functionen: the diplomatic and administrative roles performed during the revolt</term> they performed. Furthermore, as can be seen in the context of the documents, these were written and signed with their own hands. Therefore, this work <term>opus</term> or treatise <term>tractat</term> is, in and of itself and in reality <note>original Latin: "reipla," likely a contraction of "re ipsa"</note>, the aforementioned authors' own work. The only intervention has been to follow the sequence of times and events, and to relieve the reader of the burden of over-thinking, certain circumstances <note>original: "circumstantias"</note> have been explained at the beginning and end. Likewise, a few preliminary notes <note>original: "notæ"</note> have been added for information (all without any sought-after ornament or elegance).

Thus, everyone can and shall see from now on who is to be trusted and believed.

### Reader.

vor <note>This completes the word "favor" from the previous page</note> or protection this Anhalt-Palatine Chancellery <note>The "Anhalt-Pfältzische Cantzley" was a collection of captured secret documents from the Protestant leadership, published by their Catholic opponents as a "whistleblowing" exposé</note> seeks not, other than the truth and the recognition thereof, likewise justice itself, and all impartial, upright, and honest hearts—of whatever status <term>conditionen: social standing or profession</term> they may be—who have cause, both now and in the future, to take heed of this.

And because the authors of this tragedy <note>original: "Tragoedi"</note> treated these secrets so covertly, they will not be offering the slightest thanks for their disclosure; indeed, it is said that even the most prominent among those in the secret lamented this loss of the found original documents <note>original: "Originalien"</note> more than the lost kingdom, lands, and baggage <term>bagagli: personal belongings and military supplies lost during the retreat from the Battle of White Mountain</term>. Thus, those pious souls inclined toward the common welfare—especially those who were intended to suffer under these plots, or have already suffered—will be all the more obliged <note>original: "verobligiert"</note> to thank Almighty God that such schemes initiated against them and others were brought to shame and made manifest at the right time and, as the saying goes, in the midst of peril. Thus, everyone from now on can and shall see who is to be trusted and believed.

The first and third sections, however, have been gathered together afterward under a separate numbering of pages and signatures <term>buchstaben: literally "letters," referring to the printer's signatures used to mark gatherings of pages for binding</term>.

Whatever you do in secret, you do well: though you swear
The opposite of your words, so long as you bear witness: no one sees.
The evil conspiracy of the nobles against just kings,
If it is done at least in secret, it is done well: no one sees.
For the King’s destruction, to summon foreign war <note>original: "Martem" (Mars), the Roman god of war</note>
Is permitted under a hidden cloak: no one sees.
It is pleasing to incite the King’s cities and his generals,
And to overturn the world and the laws: no one sees.
"No one sees": though the conquered one sees all, once it is gained
After the victory <note>original: "palmam," referring to the palm branch given to victors in antiquity</note>. But now, tell me: "No one reads."

-># A Sincere Warning.<-

devastated, laid waste, and many places completely turned to ash; also therein so many thousands of innocent Christians’ dearly bought blood <note>This theological phrase refers to the Christian belief that human souls were "purchased" by the sacrifice of Christ; therefore, the loss of life is framed as the destruction of something precious to God.</note> has been shed, in such a way that the sorrowful remains and ruins <note>original: *vestigia & rudera*</note> are before our eyes, and will be a living sign for all posterity <note>original: *Posteris*</note>—indeed, as long as the world stands—of what has resulted in our times through our own fault and also through poorly managed actions.

Yet the source, main root, and fundamental counsels <note>original: *fundamenta consilia*</note> of all this were raised in the midst of the Roman Empire; long ago fomented, prepared, and driven forward, and finally, on the occasion of the Bohemian unrest <note>A reference to the 1618 Bohemian Revolt, the opening phase of the Thirty Years' War.</note>, fully broke out and were put into effect.

Nevertheless, it was done in such a way that the primary inventors and directors made it seem to others somewhat easy, feasible, beautiful, practical, godly, and useful in every respect. Some of these, out of a privately passionate or self-interested spirit, or as if it were a common Protestant matter <note>original: *tanquam in re communi Euangelica*. This refers to the political and religious alliances of the Protestant Union.</note>, took it entirely upon themselves; some were drawn into doubt. A good many, through plausible persuasions, were led right into the middle of the game, and also ran into such difficulties as they could not have imagined, and they themselves do not know the way to rid themselves of them.

-># A Sincere Warning.<-

Or surely, their own conscience now tells them how badly they were misled, as well as what damage, disadvantage, danger, and misery they have endured; what massive sums of money—which many a city and its citizens had saved and collected over long years with great diligence, effort, and labor—have now, within a few short years, been spent, or rather, as if thrown into the water. ->## A Sincere Warning.<-

[of the] Christian name—with much less power, expense, *preparation* <note>original: *præparation*</note>, and assembly (than has been seen over just the last two years in the Roman and neighboring empires) could have driven the enemy entirely out of Constantinople, and the Turkish provinces and the entire Orient could have been brought to Christianity.

On the contrary, all such unheard-of Christian military power <note>original: *Christliche Krigsmacht*</note> has been raised and led only among and against Christians to their own harm and ruin. When considering other candidates <note>original: *subiecta*</note>, there is admittedly no hope at this time for a Protestant leader, as that would trigger a religious war in Germany. It is not without merit that Bavaria is powerful among the Catholics and is closely befriended with the ecclesiastical and secular Prince-Electors. Accordingly, only N. <note>Frederick V of the Palatinate</note> remains; he has a large following, among whom the Jesuits have poor or even no access. For reasons of state <note>original: *per ragion distato*</note>, the Venetians <note>The Republic of Venice</note> would also gladly cooperate in this matter, and alongside England, if not helpful, they would at least not hinder the Protestants in this undertaking.

There has been a great debate regarding how they might rid themselves of the House of Austria <note>the Habsburg dynasty</note>. Most have concluded that the war should be continued and that no agreement <note>original: "accordo"</note> should be entered into with Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand II, the Holy Roman Emperor whose Catholic policies triggered the revolt</note> under any circumstances. To this end, the Bohemians have made an estimate: in the event that Ferdinand and Spain attempt to force them into obedience by power, what assistance they might expect from various sides. However, some are hesitant as to how the government <note>original: "Regiment"</note> should be established. They believe it will be difficult to make progress unless a qualified head is available, who—both by his own merit and because of his adherents <note>allies or followers</note>—is provided with such power and is so well-versed in warfare that they might be sufficiently prepared for resistance. Therefore, they would like to have a king who could not only defend them against Austria and Spain—both in Bohemia and in the incorporated lands <note>territories associated with the Bohemian Crown, such as Moravia, Silesia, and Lusatia</note>—but who could also, in case of necessity, set his foot further and enlarge the dominion <note>original: "dominum allargiern"</note>, so that the House of Austria would be weakened all the more. Others would prefer to fight for liberty, and that the Estates should henceforth no longer be subject to any king. Nevertheless, even if they did not subject themselves to any prince, they still received help from various potentates <note>foreign rulers</note>. Therefore, they are advised that for this time they should accommodate themselves with Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand II, the Habsburg claimant to the throne</note> and wait for another and better opportunity. For because the revenues of the kingdom are not particularly large, and the Estates <note>the representative assemblies of the nobility and cities</note> are not of one mind throughout, and relations with the neighbors are uncertain, they will not be able to endure the war in the long run—regardless of whether much help might have already been promised to them. Instead, when the land is ruined and uncultivated, they will at last become a prey to Ferdinand.

Others have considered it advisable that the Bohemian Estates should conduct the war on their own behalf and elect no other king, for no one would willingly risk their own lands and people for the Bohemians’ sake. They should also apply themselves to drawing Silesia, Moravia, and Austria <note>the "sister lands" of the Bohemian Crown and neighboring Habsburg territories</note> to their side. By doing so, they could block the pass <note>strategic mountain passes or transit routes</note> to the Hungarians, so that they cannot be used to the detriment of the Bohemian Estates, since the Hungarians are showing themselves to be so strongly in favor of the Austrians. No less should the Unionists <note>the Protestant Union, a coalition of Protestant German states</note> apply themselves to taking the pass in Alsace away from Archduke Leopold, so that the troops from Spain and the Netherlands cannot be let through those places. For when all passes are taken from Ferdinand, the Bohemian Estates can easily maintain their freedom without a king and, moreover, bring more lands under their power. Thus, it is concluded that the Bohemians should make themselves into free Estates <note>a republic similar to the Dutch model</note>; then they will obtain all help and assistance from the Dutch, as well as from the Imperial Cities and several potentates who are not well-disposed toward the House of Austria. Just as it appears clearly enough from the six letters of Camerarius <note>Ludwig Camerarius, a chief advisor to the Elector Palatine</note> and the Lord High Steward from 1619, which we have just heard, with what thoughts and plans they operated in Frankfurt during the ongoing election, and how the Calvinist faction <note>The Protestant party supporting the Elector Palatine, Frederick V</note> would have liked to direct matters—as the memorandum drawn up in Crailsheim on March 19, 1619 (noted above on folio 72) indicates—namely, because they could not prevent the election day itself, they intended at the very least that no election be held there, and that Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand II, the Catholic Habsburg candidate and future Emperor</note> should by no means be summoned or admitted to it. 

Toward this goal, they had already made good preparations <term>preparations|original: *præparatoria*; preliminary diplomatic groundwork or maneuvers</term> with Trier through the mediation of the French Crown (as the memorandum shows), and the Brandenburg vote was already at the disposal of the Palatinate <note>The Elector of Brandenburg was a fellow Protestant ally</note>. 

Meanwhile, they were not idle in Prague either; rather, Achatz von Dohna <note>A prominent diplomat and soldier serving the Palatinate</note>—for the other privy councilors <term>privy councilors|High-ranking, confidential advisors to a sovereign</term> were in Frankfurt, while at Amberg, no one was with the Count Palatine except Anhalt and Ansbach—proceeded quite zealously with his commission in Prague, which contained the following: First, to solicit the abdication <note>The formal removal or rejection of Ferdinand II from the Bohemian throne by the Bohemian Estates</note>, and immediately thereafter the notification <term>notification|original: *intimation*; a formal announcement to a legal body</term> of said abdication to the Electoral College; then, to procure the election <note>The election of Frederick V as the new King of Bohemia</note> of the Count Palatine in such a way that, if possible, such an intended election should not be published until one could see where the election—

Of particular note was how the Fourth Estate <note>The peasantry or commoners</note>, four hundred men strong, received the new king near the newly built entrenchment. They carried an old banner featuring the name of Žižka <note>Jan Žižka, the legendary Hussite general who fought the Imperial forces two centuries earlier</note>, along with paintings of the chalice and the Host <note>Central symbols of the Hussite faith, representing the layperson's right to receive both bread and wine during communion</note>. They were equipped with old, heavy breastplates and **helmets** <note>original: *Pickelhauben*</note>, blunt **halberds** <note>original: *hellenbarten*</note>, iron **flails** <note>original: *Drischlen*; these were traditional Hussite peasant weapons</note>, crossbows, and large shields. Standing in battle formation, they received the Count Palatine with a Latin **speech** <note>original Latin: *oration*</note>. As they made a great clatter with their weapons, they moved the Count Palatine to laughter (to the singular honor of the German nation and the Roman Empire, **in memory** <note>original Latin: *in memoriam*</note> of that which occurred years ago **under Sigismund** <note>The text likely refers to Emperor Sigismund and the beginning of the Hussite Wars, drawing a parallel between that historical chaos and the present rebellion</note>...

As for why Ansbach proposed this *enterprise*, this was the reason: because he had received a letter from the people of Nuremberg, in which they promised great deeds <note>literally "offered great strokes"</note> they were willing to perform for the Union, provided that matters were not so *precipitated* <note>acted upon with too much haste</note>.

On the 24th of the same month, a dispatch was sent from the High Steward <note>Likely Count Hans Albrecht von Solms, a key diplomat for the Palatinate</note> to the Prince of Anhalt <note>Christian I of Anhalt-Bernburg, the chief advisor to Frederick V</note>. It was strongly feared that the Imperial proposal—especially since they were dealing with some parties *privately* <note>original: "ad partem"</note>—might provoke an *alteration* <note>meaning a change or shift in loyalty</note> among the Estates. Therefore, the Palatine Councillors—as can be understood from another letter *dated* <note>original: "de dato"</note> the 25th of November—have prepared the ground well with the Estates so that such an *embassy* <note>original: "ambasciata"</note> would end without fruit. They did this under the pretext that Spanish tricks and *artifices* <note>clever deceptions or maneuvers</note> were involved, and that the intent was to divide the Estates through these means, etc.

<margin>NB.</margin>
The High Steward further complains about the Estates of the Union <note>The Protestant Union, a coalition of Protestant German states</note>, noting that they have insisted quite vehemently on demanding the return of the Union’s troops. (Elsewhere it is written that the Union claims not to be interested in the Bohemian business.) These were the troops that the Count Palatine <note>Frederick V, Elector Palatine and newly crowned King of Bohemia</note> had taken with him into Bohemia. The Estates insist they should no longer be used in Bohemia, so as not to create the appearance that they were openly and *directly* <note>original: "directè"</note> making themselves a party to that conflict. Alternatively, if the Count Palatine were to keep the Union’s troops in Bohemia, the Margrave of Ansbach <note>Joachim Ernst of Brandenburg-Ansbach, the military commander of the Union</note> should be permitted to recruit other troops to fill the positions left vacant within the Union, etc. Some among the Union members are also suggesting that the Count Palatine should now waive the 6,000 guilders that the Union had granted him monthly for his *Generalship* <note>original: "Generalat"; the supreme military command</note>. The Count Palatine has little desire for this, which has led to several instances of *discontent*. Thus, they are currently at work trying to figure out how to escape this *labyrinth* <note>A metaphor for the complex and trapped diplomatic situation</note>.

Without any doubt, [this was proposed] because not only the Duke, but even more so the other Catholics, were perceived by those of the Union <note>The Protestant Union, a coalition of Protestant German states</note> in the draft as being fearful, having always fled from war and unrest rather than surrendering a portion of the archdioceses and foundations <note>*Erz- und Stiffter* — ecclesiastical territories ruled by Prince-Bishops</note>, lands, and people, so that they might only remain in peace with the remainder. But especially before all this, various intelligences, correspondences, alliances, and treaties were concluded in different places, both within and outside the Empire, by means of which the **Papists** <note>Catholics</note> in the known locations were to "draw the shorter straw" <note>to be defeated or disadvantaged</note>.

They had already seen (Note Well) a small sign of this during the last war, along with other similar circumstances.

Similarly, the Administration <note>the office managing secularized church properties, such as monasteries and parishes</note> is entirely void of money because, at present, wine and grain cannot be sold for any cash, and the Administration's income consists solely of these two commodities.

<meta>This page continues the diplomatic correspondence from King James I of England to his son-in-law, Frederick V of the Palatinate. The King is explaining his refusal to formally recognize Frederick's new title as King of Bohemia, fearing that such a move would trigger a massive religious conflict across Europe.</meta>

309

# ->Sincere Warning.<-

<margin>July 1620.</margin>...had reasonable concerns about declaring himself in favor of the Count Palatine <term>Pfalzgraf: the title of Frederick V, ruler of the Rhine Palatinate and James I's son-in-law</term> in this matter, so that they might not, by their example, provoke other princes—who until now have remained strictly neutral—to likewise join in this business, and specifically on the opposing side. From this, nothing else would have resulted but a general Religious War, to the extreme scandal and obvious danger of all Christendom. This is why he, the King [James I], must still persist in this resolution and apply himself far more to pouring oil into the wounds <note>In the 17th century, "pouring oil" was understood as a medicinal act of healing and soothing a wound, rather than the modern idiom of adding fuel to a fire</note> so that, if possible, the evil may be soothed and healed through the mediation <term>interposition: diplomatic intervention by a third party to resolve a conflict</term> he has applied here, rather than making the misfortune even greater by declaring himself for one party.

And although the first attempt the King made through Viscount Doncaster <note>James Hay, 1st Earl of Carlisle, an experienced diplomat sent to mediate between the Bohemians and the Emperor</note> for this purpose did not reach the success he desired, he nevertheless does not wish to cease offering further mediation. This is all the more so because it appears there is now a somewhat better hope for a fruitful effect, as time has matured these matters in the interim and spirits have become better disposed toward reconciliation. He revealed that if Upper Austria were to be occupied and overwhelmed, it would then be the end for the Lower Austrians <note>original: *Vnder Enser*</note> as well. In this way, a passage would be opened into all the confederated kingdoms and lands, such that they—and especially Hungary—would fall into utter ruin, and everyone would be forced to submit and surrender to the will of the Emperor <note>Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II</note>.

In response, Gábor <note>Gabriel Bethlen, the Prince of Transylvania and leader of the Hungarian uprising</note> answered with visible emotion, speaking partly through a secretary's translation and partly in Latin. He stated that he felt a particular sympathy for them, but they should not despair of God or the means of help. He already had over 5,000 Hungarian cavalrymen stationed "above" <note>likely meaning further north or in the highlands</note> near the Prince of Anhalt. He expressed his surprise that they remained so still and accomplished nothing with such a significant force <note>original: *ansehenlichem Volck*</note>.

Gábor noted that he had written to the King of Bohemia <note>Frederick V, the Elector Palatine, known as the "Pfalzgraf"</note> regarding this matter, suggesting that early precautions be taken against an invasion. To this, the King of Bohemia replied that he had 7,000 men in those regions under Count Thurn and Mansfeld <note>Major Protestant military commanders</note> for the purpose of intercepting the Duke of Bavaria and Archduke Leopold at the Golden Path <note>original: *Guldensteig*; a strategic mountain pass between Bohemia and Bavaria</note> and bringing relief to Upper Austria.

At this point, Gábor asked how strong the forces of Bavaria and Leopold were. The envoys replied: six regiments and 2,000 cavalry. Gábor remarked that such an army <note>original: *exercitu*</note> could certainly still be countered. He advised that the members of the noble Estates should move their wives and children to secure places, and that the peasants should save themselves and their belongings by fleeing to the forests and mountains, the

But how poorly the Elector of Brandenburg is now situated—placed, as it were, in the middle between two kings, one of whom he must necessarily offend—is something the Palatine Count, in his great wisdom, can well judge. Indeed, it might have been manageable if such a marriage had been handled with good discretion; however, since they proceeded so <term>precipitously</term> <note>original: "præcipitanter"; meaning headlong or without due caution</note> in this matter, the Elector has fallen into the utmost difficulty, from which he will not be able to extricate himself so easily. # ->Sincere Warning<-

It is surprising to see how industrious, diligent, subtle, and tireless the Calvinist spirit is, and in what many various forms it operates in all places—even in Rome with the Pope, in France, Spain, Savoy, Venice, etc. They manage to establish connections and find secret correspondents and informants <note>original: *Kundtschaffter*</note> who investigate other potentates, Electors <term>Electors (Chur-Fürsten): High-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire with the right to elect the Emperor.</term>, communities, and lordships. They must uphold and maintain these, ensuring that none should molest, disturb, or cause injury to another in what is theirs.

Furthermore, with collective counsel and action, they must resist to the best of their ability the unchristian and ever-persisting **Calvinist spirit**. This spirit has not only maintained <term>correspondenz</term> <note>correspondence or secret communication</note> with the **Hereditary Enemy** <note>The Ottoman Empire</note> and its <term>Creatur</term> <note>minions or agents</note>, seeking help and <term>protection</term> there and attempting all manner of <term>extrema tentirt</term> <note>extreme measures</note>, but it has even aimed for and advised such desperation that it now openly—and even at the courts of **Prince-Electors**, as the **Count of Hohenlohe** recently threatened and <term>protested</term> in **Saxony**—proclaims that if its demands are not <term>condescendirt</term> <note>yielded to</note>, it will actually bring in the **Turks** and **Tatars**.

->and<-

<summary>The author calls for imperial unity under the Emperor and the legal framework of the Peace of Augsburg, while accusing Calvinists of treasonous plots with the Ottoman Empire.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Roman Empire, Peace of Augsburg, Calvinism, Ottoman Empire, Count of Hohenlohe, Saxony, Imperial Constitutions</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the pamphlet's warning, arguing that the Calvinist movement is a pretext for dismantling the Holy Roman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy, potentially delivering Europe into the hands of the Ottoman Empire.</meta>

<header>
### A Sincere Warning
</header>

...and thus protect the **Holy Roman Empire**, itself, its <term>posteros</term> <note>original: "posteros"; descendants or posterity</note>, land, and people from the beastly <term>servitut</term> <note>original: "servitut"; servitude</note> of the **Hereditary Enemy** <note>A common term for the Ottoman Empire</note>, as well as preserve the distressed lands from total ruin.

And the whole world must see that—while the **Calvinist spirit** seeks to blind everyone (as its <term>actiones</term> <note>original: "actiones"; actions</note> are only directed toward the subversion of the **Austrian** and **Spanish monarchy**)—it presumes, under this false <term>prætext</term> <note>pretext</note>, to <term>inuertirn</term> <note>original: "inuertirn"; to invert or overturn</note> the **Holy Roman Empire** along with its magnificent ordinances: to introduce a new Calvinist rule: and to promote the establishment of a truly Calvinist, or ultimately even a **Turkish** <term>dominat</term> <note>dominion or rule</note>. It attempts to deliver worthy Christendom into the maw and servitude of the **Hereditary Enemy**, with the loss of both temporal and eternal welfare—which God Almighty, in response to the imploring sighs of pious Christians, will surely turn away and cast back upon the **Calvinist spirit**—and it is indeed fully at work in this, etc.

-> T H E  E N D . <-

---

-> Printed in the Old Town of **Prague**, by **Tobias** <-
-> **Leopoldt**. In the year 1621. <-

<summary>This final page of the 1621 pamphlet warns that Calvinist political ambitions threaten to dismantle the Holy Roman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy, ultimately risking Christian subjugation by the Ottoman Empire. It concludes with the publication details of Tobias Leopoldt in Prague.</summary>
